questions.question: In an older patient with prior transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) who now has dyspnoea, a rising mean transvalvular gradient, and moderate-to-severe intraprosthetic regurgitation, what are the leading causes of transcatheter prosthetic valve dysfunction (e.g., structural valve deterioration, leaflet thrombosis, prosthetic valve endocarditis, malposition/underexpansion, prosthesis–patient mismatch), and which clinical or echocardiographic features help distinguish among them?

When prosthetic valve endocarditis is suspected after TAVI, what is the recommended diagnostic workup, and how do the modified Duke criteria incorporate blood cultures, transoesophageal echocardiography, and adjunct imaging (cardiac CT and FDG-PET/CT) to establish the diagnosis?

Before planning a TAV-in-TAV (or TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV) procedure, which CT-based measurements stratify the risk of coronary obstruction and sinus sequestration, and what threshold values would prompt coronary protection or leaflet modification strategies (e.g., valve-to-coronary distance, coronary ostial height, sinus of Valsalva dimensions, sinotubular junction height/virtual valve-to-STJ distance, and virtual transcatheter valve-to-coronary distance)?

Given a minimal internal lumen diameter of approximately 14 mm within a prior TAVR frame, which transcatheter valve design features (e.g., supra-annular leaflet position, frame height and cell geometry, radial force) and implantation strategies (e.g., high implantation, commissural alignment) help maximise effective orifice area and preserve future coronary access for a third valve?

How do you interpret an immediate post-implant mean gradient of 67 mm Hg with a calculated aortic valve area of 0.9 cm², indexed area 0.4 cm²/m², and a Doppler velocity index (DVI) of 0.24 after a third TAVI, and what intra- and early post-procedural steps help differentiate severe prosthesis–patient mismatch from valve underexpansion or high-flow states?

What pathophysiological mechanisms link a prior episode of prosthetic valve endocarditis—after microbiologic cure—to subsequent leaflet dysfunction and restenosis (consider leaflet fibrosis/scar, commissural restriction, pannus, and interaction with sequential valve-in-valve frames)?

In a patient with treated Enterococcus faecalis prosthetic valve endocarditis, two prior TAVR frames integrated into the aortic root, prohibitive surgical risk (e.g., EuroSCORE II ~27%), and multiple comorbidities, what multidisciplinary considerations and guideline principles support redo TAVI over surgical explantation/aortic root replacement?

During redo TAVI in stacked frames, which intra-procedural strategies mitigate coronary obstruction—choice of valve type (supra-annular vs intra-annular), commissural alignment, high vs low implantation depth, pre-emptive coronary protection (wires/‘chimney’ stents), and leaflet laceration (BASILICA)—and when would you choose each approach?

What antithrombotic regimen is recommended after TAVI for a patient without atrial fibrillation but with a history of recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding, and what evidence or guideline rationale supports that choice over alternatives?

For long-term surveillance after a TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV, which clinical and echocardiographic parameters and time points should be monitored to detect structural valve deterioration and prosthesis–patient mismatch, and how would you interpret a stable mean gradient of ~26–27 mm Hg with an aortic valve area of ~1.1 cm² at 1 year in an asymptomatic patient?

Three months after a TAV-in-TAV, a patient presents with fever and a new mean gradient rise to 35 mm Hg. Which bedside findings, laboratory results, and imaging features help discriminate leaflet thrombosis from prosthetic valve endocarditis, and how would initial management differ between these two entities?
